rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human and jinn leaders of deception cast their inspiration as philosophies and communicate it in varied ways; the Qur’an calls such deceivers devils.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has used the word devil for all such leaders of deception.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word marīd means mischievous, miscreant, or wretched; devils pose as sincere well-wishers, lead servants astray, and bring followers who spread their mischief to Hell.
rows.anchor: These devils, whether they belong to jinn or men always appear in the garb of sincere well-wishers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism follows the Hereafter because accepting partners or intercessors makes accountability seem insignificant; the adjacent themes show that none can save people from God’s grasp, and He alone judges.
rows.anchor: Monotheism is mentioned right after the Day of Judgement because the latter’s importance is related to the former.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan received respite until Judgement to lead Adam’s descendants astray; this is his assigned duty, but only those who befriend him fall under his influence.
rows.anchor: God had granted him this respite after which He will consign him and all his followers to the fire of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who treat Satan as an enemy and guard against his mischief are not affected by his lures, just as only a fool takes poison for an antidote.
rows.anchor: Those who regard him to be their enemy and always try to shield themselves from his mischief will not be impacted by his luring.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s respite for Satan tests people; it is not permission to make Satan their guide, receive inspiration from him, or follow him.
rows.anchor: God has given this respite to Satan to test people and not to make him their leader and receive inspiration from him or to follow him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage revisits monotheism and the Hereafter through human creation, cosmic signs, and divine attributes, contrasts sincere submission with conditional worship and hypocrisy, and concludes with the fate of believers and polytheists.
rows.anchor: In the coming verses, the subject of monotheism and hereafter discussed earlier is brought up in another way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation’s stages, observable signs in the universe, and the divine attributes they reveal argue for monotheism and resurrection; reflection on oneself and the surrounding world suffices to see these clear truths.
rows.anchor: He does not need to go far.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some people worship on their own terms: they comply when directives suit their desires but evade those that conflict with their interests, becoming two-faced hypocrites.
rows.anchor: As long as His directives were in accordance with their desires, they were prepared to worship Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites seek to believe in God and Satan, belief and disbelief together; their conciliatory posture is effectively polytheism, even worse than open opposition, and religion permits no such double standards.
rows.anchor: It wanted to believe in God and Satan, belief and disbelief at the same time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deny that benefit and harm are in God’s hands may choose their conduct, but their strategies cannot succeed without His consent; believers and polytheists will face judgement according to belief and deeds.
rows.anchor: the greatest of their strategies is not going to avail them without God’s consent.

none: English translation of the verses only.
English translation of the verses only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idolaters doubted resurrection because they considered revival after bodily decay implausible; hypothetical belief left them relying on deities and intercessors to evade accountability.
rows.anchor: they thought it was very unlikely for people to be raised to life again after they die and their bodies are decomposed into mud.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an insists the Hereafter is real life and this world its prelude and necessary consequence, while proving that the supposed deities and intercessors have no basis.
rows.anchor: the real life is that of the hereafter; it iterated that this world is a prelude and the next one is its necessary consequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeling their position threatened, the idolaters harassed the Prophet, demanding the promised doom or a tangible punishment as proof.
rows.anchor: the only antidote they had to salvage the situation was to harass and corner the Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an answers their doubts by directing them to human development and everyday observations: attentive people can see proof of God’s oneness and the Hereafter within themselves and around them.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has directed their attention to their own phases of creation and everyday observations of the world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlaqah can mean a clot of blood or a small living insect; it is the womb stage after sperm when the embryo takes a blood-like form and shows signs of life.
rows.anchor: This phase comes after the sperm is lodged in the womb when it assumes the shape of blood and a foetus, and shows signs of life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muḍghah means a lump of flesh at the next fetal stage; some reach final form and others remain defective by God’s will, which no one can rectify.
rows.anchor: This is the stage following the previous one when the foetus assumes the form of a lump of flesh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stages of human development are not needed for God to create; He could make fully formed people at once, but chose this process to teach people His power, wisdom, and providence.
rows.anchor: God was not dependent on all these phases in order to create human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human creation testifies that people were not made for amusement but for a purpose that will become manifest; the Creator who made life from clay and fluid can readily resurrect it.
rows.anchor: his own being bears witness that He Who has created him in such an elaborate manner and shown favour to him has not made him a toy for amusement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation sequence in al-Mu’minūn describes the same reality as this passage and summarizes the stages that testify to resurrection.
rows.anchor: The following verses of Sūrah al-Mu’minūn point to precisely the same reality:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Modern philosophers and scientists observe the developmental stages but fail to grasp the divine purpose of this arrangement.
rows.anchor: do observe all these phases of creation but they are not able to grasp the actual purpose for which God has made all this arrangement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about keeping a fetus in the womb until an appointed time is followed by an insertion that interrupts the discourse to caution and awaken its addressees, after which it resumes.
rows.anchor: The discourse was still going on when suddenly the words i were inserted in it to caution and prod the addressees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inserted phrase ‘whatever We want’ emphasizes that a child’s sex, appearance, and whether it is defective or perfect are wholly determined by God.
rows.anchor: The words “whatever We want” show whether the child is a girl or a boy, attractive or ugly, defective or perfect entirely rests on God’s will.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The duration of pregnancy also lies within God’s discretion, and no one else can change it.
rows.anchor: Similarly, the time of pregnancy is also in God’s discretion and none has the authority to change its duration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām signals a suppressed verb: God lets a newborn gradually reach maturity, and no one can skip the stages of childhood.
rows.anchor: God gives time to the newly born child to gradually reach maturity and this pattern is always followed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A suppressed parallel expression means many die in childhood or adolescence while others reach extreme old age; lifespan is entirely under God’s authority.
rows.anchor: many human beings die in chidhood and adolescence and many who reach the exteme of old age.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite ‘knowledge’ can signify belittlement or magnification; the author prefers that old age erases the little knowledge one acquired, supported by 17:85, and warns knowledge is God-given and can be taken away.
rows.anchor: I would give preference to the first of these interpretations as parallel verses corroborate it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dry earth revived by rain is an external sign of resurrection; people repeatedly witness this pattern, so the omitted words need not be repeated because the sign is obvious.
rows.anchor: After directing attention to the signs of the Day of Judgement found within the stages of creation of human beings, the external world is focused upon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 7 summarizes the sūrah’s argument to this point: God alone is real, resurrection is within His power, and the creation of people and revival of earth show that re-creation is easy for Him.
rows.anchor: This verse presents a summary of what is stated in the sūrah from the beginning up to this point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 8 explains the disputation introduced in verse 3: idolaters acknowledge God while associating partners, yet have no proof for those partners and rely only on ancestral custom and refusal to bear humiliation.
rows.anchor: The onus of proof of their existence was on them but they never had any.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their debate is driven by arrogance and blind ancestral loyalty, which reason cannot affect; the Qur’an calls such argumentation groundless, as 40:56 and 31:20–21 illustrate.
rows.anchor: Obviously, when a debate hinges merely upon blind following of ancestors, it amounts to arrogance and haughtiness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away while shaking one’s shoulders depicts arrogance; lacking evidence and refusing to abandon a position, disputants answer the dent to their pride with a show of haughtiness.
rows.anchor: When a person turns away in arrogance, he shakes his shoulders while turning away.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their pride aims to mislead others; a person aware of having gone astray may still return, but an arrogant imposer of baseless ideas offers no hope of good.
rows.anchor: All this pride is not meant to support some truth but only to lead people astray just like themselves have gone astray.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger’s addressees face worldly subjugation and humiliation if they persist after decisive communication of truth, followed by Hell in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: in their case the established practice of God is that if these people become adamant on opposing the truth after its conclusive communication

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire punishment mirrors the anger, hatred, and jealousy with which they burned in this life.
rows.anchor: since in this world they burned and seethed in anger, hate and jealousy, they will face the torment of buring in the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about God not being unjust suppresses ‘it will be said’; their punishment itself will show that it is the consequence of their own deeds.
rows.anchor: the situation itself will bear witness that what they see is the result of the seeds they had sown

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic form of ‘unjust’ under negation intensifies the denial: God is not in the least unjust; people reap in the Hereafter what they sow, and anger against truth leads to Hell.
rows.anchor: God is not the slightest unjust to His servants.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 11 turns from open advocates of polytheism to opportunists who try to maintain ties with both God and Satan, truth and falsehood; after Islam’s rise, two-faced people appeared among idolaters and the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: After mentioning the Idolaters who were prepared to argue and debate in favour of polytheism, those people are referred to who wanted to simultaneously have ties with God and Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These opportunists sought a compromise between belief and disbelief, keeping ancestral deities for their supposed benefits; even when they entered Islam, calamity drove them to other protectors, making their posture polytheism.
rows.anchor: They reckoned that why should these beings be forsaken when they are of benefit to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference between these hypocrites and aggressive polytheist debaters is only tone; genuine monotheism requires total submission whether God grants comfort or decrees a terrible death.
rows.anchor: If there is a difference between the two, it is only of the tone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Worshipping God at one edge’ expresses disgust: worship means servitude and obedience, while ‘edge’ means from afar; such people neither fully enter Islam nor sincerely side with Muslims or disbelievers, as the cited verses illustrate.
rows.anchor: The word “worship” here refers both to servitude and obedience to the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fitnah means trial or calamity and explains their wavering: they are content while things suit them, but flee adversity; the path to God includes trials that must be passed to please Him.
rows.anchor: This portion is actually an explanation of the words “at an edge.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trials that are met with submission strengthen faith and multiply future reward; those who despair of God and think ill of Him lose both worlds, while ordinary worldly loss can be recompensed in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: All such trials strengthen his faith and multiply his reward manifold in the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author applies the verse to Muslims today: they may revere the Qur’an ceremonially yet follow others in public and private affairs and use the Qur’an at funerals instead of as guidance for the living.
rows.anchor: For them, the Qur’ ān is not a Book for the living; it is a Book for the dead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ‘invoke’ includes praying, pleading, beseeching, and seeking help or mercy; assigning another being authority to harm or benefit is polytheism, since only God controls this and all reliance should be on Him.
rows.anchor: If someone is invoked thinking that he has the authority to cause harm or benefit, then this is polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable in 22:73 shows the extreme error of seeking refuge with beings unable even to create a fly or recover what it steals; fleeing God’s trial thus ends in Hell.
rows.anchor: Those who you invoke besides God cannot even create a fly in spite of all of them trying to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers grammarians who read the second ‘invoke’ as a repetition of the previous verse’s verb, expressing sorrow and yearning rather than governing the following phrase.
rows.anchor: The repetition of the verb is only for the purpose of expresssing sorrow and yearning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this grammatical reading, ‘those whose harm is nearer than their benefit’ supplements the previous object and explains what makes the invocation extreme error.
